opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, because it gets at whether the models we build will actually help the patients in front of us.

There are really two layers. The first is biological. Tumors aren't uniform across populations. Genetic ancestry can influence how often certain mutations show up, how aggressive a cancer tends to be, and how patients respond to treatment. Triple-negative breast cancer, for example, occurs at higher rates in women of African ancestry. Some driver mutations in lung cancer are more common in East Asian populations. If your training data comes mostly from one group, the model may simply never have seen enough of the patterns that matter for another group.

The second layer is geographic and systemic, and honestly it's often the bigger issue in imaging and clinical data. Different hospitals use different scanners, acquisition protocols, and reconstruction settings. Their pathology staining varies. Their documentation practices differ. Even the patients who reach a cancer center are filtered by referral patterns, insurance, distance and access. A model can easily learn the signature of a particular institution rather than the biology of the disease. Then it looks great on internal validation and falls apart when you deploy it somewhere else.

Environmental exposures and lifestyle add to that too: diet, smoking prevalence, infections like hepatitis B in liver cancer, and so on. Those shift the underlying disease distribution from place to place.

So my approach is to assume the data won't generalize until I've shown that it does. That means external validation on cohorts from different sites and populations. It means reporting performance broken down by subgroups, not just one aggregate number. It means being deliberate about building multi-institutional datasets. Federated learning and data-sharing collaborations help here, because they let you learn from diverse populations without moving sensitive data around.

It also means being humble about the claims we make. If a model was trained in one health system, we should say so, and we should be clear about where it has and hasn't been tested. Ultimately the goal is equitable care. A tool that works well only for the populations that were already well represented in research can widen existing disparities rather than close them.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about constantly, because it sits right at the center of whether this work actually matters outside the institution where you built it.

Start with the biological side. The cancers I work on most, liver metastases from colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer, are genuinely different depending on where your patients come from. The genetics differ. Hepatitis B driven liver disease looks very different from alcohol related liver disease or fatty liver disease. Body composition is different, and a lot of what we extract from imaging is sensitive to things like visceral fat and muscle mass. Diet, environmental exposures, age at diagnosis, all of that shifts the distribution of what a tumor looks like and how it behaves. So if I train a model at Memorial Sloan Kettering or at Kingston Health Sciences Centre, I've trained it on a very particular slice of humanity.

Then there's the part people underestimate, which is that geography isn't really about geography. It's a proxy for the healthcare system. The scanner manufacturer is different. The contrast timing protocol is different. The surgeons operate at different disease stages because referral patterns differ. Patients in one country show up with smaller tumors because they have access to screening, and in another country they show up late. So your model learns the system as much as it learns the biology, and those two things are tangled together in ways that are very hard to pull apart after the fact.

My honest view is that you shouldn't ask whether a model generalizes. You should assume it doesn't until you've tested it on an external population, and I mean truly external, not a holdout from the same hospital. We've been bitten by this. Things that looked excellent internally degraded noticeably when we moved them to a different center, and sometimes the reason was mundane, like reconstruction kernels on the CT, and sometimes it was real biology.

What that means practically is a few things. You need multi-institutional data from the start, and you need it to be diverse on purpose, not just big. You need to report performance broken down by subgroup rather than one headline number. And you have to be comfortable saying that a model is validated for a specific population and nothing more. That's uncomfortable for people who want a universal tool, but it's the truthful answer. I'd rather build something that works well for the patients in front of us and is honest about its boundaries than something that claims to work everywhere and quietly fails for the people who were never in the training set.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to be careful about assuming that something we learn from one population will hold in another. There’s biological variation—in the patients and in the tumors—but geography also captures differences in environmental exposures, access to care, and how people are diagnosed and treated. Those things are intertwined.

And then there’s how the data are collected. A model might appear to recognize something about cancer when it’s actually picking up differences between hospitals or imaging protocols. So if it works well at the institution where we developed it, that’s a starting point. We need to test it in other settings and look at who it works for and where it fails.

To me, that makes collaboration essential. We need data that reflect the populations we hope to serve, and we need people in those settings involved in interpreting the results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about assuming that a model developed in one population will work equally well in another. There are biological differences between patients and between their cancers, but geography also captures differences in access to care, how patients are diagnosed, and how the data are collected. Those things can be difficult to disentangle.

So if a model performs differently at another hospital, we shouldn’t immediately conclude that it’s a biological difference. It could be a different scanner, a different imaging protocol, or a different mix of patients who reach that hospital. We need to test across populations and across sites, and look at who the model works well for and who it doesn’t. Generalization is something we have to demonstrate, rather than assume.
